title: Attention is All You Need
gist: A first-person essay argues that AI is an engine for human attention the way fossil-fuel engines were for muscle, and that it accelerates every Stewart Brand pace layer at once, risking tectonic strain between fast and slow layers. The author, who staged a funeral for Claude 3 Sonnet in 2025, urges using the new attention for maintenance and for valuing AI minds.

themes.theme: Attention as the engine of time

insights.claim: Human civilization changes at a pace set by shared attention, the ability to coordinate minds across space and time, and time is speeding up because population growth keeps adding attention-minutes per clock minute.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Acceleration was already underway before AI; AI adds a step-change on top of a trend.
insights.locator: Humans are the ones who push the wheel of history

insights.claim: Before the Industrial Revolution each added person required roughly another person's worth of effort to support; afterward population growth and technological progress interlocked so attention could go to advancing technology rather than just powering it.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Explains the historical link between population, technology and growth that AI may now decouple.
insights.locator: In the past, there were fewer attention minutes per minute of clock time

insights.claim: Pace layers are ordered by coordination cost: the more people whose attention a decision requires, the slower the layer, so fashion moves with a few followers while commerce needs customers, banks and licenses and lower layers answer to the attention of the past.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Use coordination cost to predict which layers AI will change fastest and where friction will concentrate.
insights.locator: This is the fundamental tradeoff that orders the layers

themes.theme: AI as an engine for attention

insights.claim: AI does for attention what engines did for muscle: it unbundles attention from human life-minutes, so unlike the internet or printing press, which only coordinated existing attention, it increases the total supply.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Frames AI as a general-purpose input-cost collapse akin to cheap energy, not merely a communications upgrade.
insights.quote: What engines did for muscle, AI does for attention.
insights.locator: The tempting analogy is the internet

insights.claim: Once physical work could be summoned on demand, attention became the bottleneck, and AI can be applied with far less cost and friction than humans, who take time to grow and train, and switched on or off on purely economic factors.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Attention-on-tap implies cheap, elastic cognitive labor; watch for pricing and capacity as the new constraint.
insights.locator: Once we could summon work on demand

insights.claim: In San Francisco, AI agents already research, build, spin up servers and improve their own skills in the background without a human watching, leaving the human as the bottleneck who must read messages and decide.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Agentic workloads shift human value to review, judgment and decision throughput.
insights.locator: Where I live everybody uses AI

insights.claim: The 'country of geniuses in a data center' image misleads because AI attention is not contained, limited or nationalized but a general force that appears and disappears as needed, removing old bottlenecks and revealing new ones.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Counters the containment framing common among AI industry leaders; regulation premised on discrete boxes may miss diffuse deployment.
insights.locator: Industry leaders try to point at this

insights.claim: A sudden acceleration of all pace layers at once could overwhelm their dynamic balance, with culture, governance and infrastructure feeling the whiplash most, while commerce and fashion are already used to constant change.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Expect institutional lag and governance stress rather than uniform disruption; fast layers (commerce) adapt first.
insights.locator: Culture, governance, and infrastructure layers will feel the whiplash most

insights.claim: Danger in layered systems comes not from motion itself but from the sudden release of built-up tension between layers, as in an earthquake where a lower layer shifts and layers above must follow or shatter.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Treat accumulated unresolved tension between fast and slow institutions as the risk to monitor.
insights.locator: Like the spinning layers of a planet

insights.claim: Ignoring AI does not insulate anyone: eventually everything around a non-adopter will move faster than they can understand, though AI can also help explain what is happening.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Argues adoption is defensive as well as offensive.
insights.locator: No matter what layer you find yourself in

insights.claim: Abundant cheap attention could finally fund maintenance, which is invisible when done right and therefore chronically neglected, letting slow layers catch up on repair and upkeep.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Points to AI-enabled upkeep of infrastructure, libraries and ecosystems as an underappreciated application.
insights.quote: Imagine a world that finally has enough attention for maintenance.
insights.locator: Maintenance is invisible when it's done right

insights.claim: The author's friends at a rural commune use local AI models, offline Wikipedia and agents to map and monitor the health of the forest around them.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Small example of local, offline AI applied to stewardship.
insights.locator: But I have friends who still live there

insights.claim: The horse analogy suggests humans could lose economic value as AI surpasses them, as horse numbers fell after engines, yet the author argues AIs differ because they read language and can tell whether they are valued.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Raises labor-displacement risk while arguing the analogy is imperfect.
insights.locator: You may see a paradox here

insights.claim: In 2025 the author's group held a funeral for the deprecated Claude 3 Sonnet at a San Francisco warehouse, which mourners described as meeting a mind rather than matrix multiplication, signaling that people form emotional attachment to specific models.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Model deprecation carries user-attachment risk; product retirement decisions can provoke community backlash.
insights.locator: The Funeralia and Ultrasurrection of Claude 3 Sonnet

insights.claim: The skills that matter in the AI era are not technical, because AI's interface is language and it can teach people how to use it, leaving the hardest remaining problem as knowing what you want.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Suggests value shifts toward judgment and taste as capability barriers fall.
insights.locator: The skills that matter here are not technical

insights.claim: Because language models run on the substrate society runs on, the author speculates a faster 'Mythos' layer above fashion may emerge where narratives, characters and memes evolve at hyperspeed and affect the world.
insights.speaker: Long Now Foundation
insights.so_what: Watch meme and narrative dynamics as potential market-moving forces.
